meta: Nexora Lab brings host metrics, Proxmox guests, Docker workloads and alerts into a self-hosted dashboard. Explore its architecture and release limits.
overview: Nexora Lab is a self-hosted infrastructure dashboard for inspecting Linux hosts, Proxmox guests and Docker workloads. Telemetry, history and topology connect resource readings with the systems they describe.
problem: A host list does not explain how virtual machines, containers and physical resources relate. The project addresses that visibility gap: it connects changing metrics with the systems they describe, so an administrator can inspect a host in context.
approach: The React interface receives real-time updates from an Express backend over WebSocket. The backend combines Nexora Agent telemetry with optional direct Proxmox data and persists application records in SQLite. The interface does not need to know which collector supplied an individual metric.
features: Host metrics, history charts, topology and alerts
Optional Proxmox integration and complementary Agent data
Role-based administrator controls and documented recovery tools
result: Reviewed source implements the dashboard, telemetry model and administration workflow. The original dashboard capture is withheld because it contains private host details; it is not evidence that every collector is connected to a live deployment.
tradeoff: Available telemetry depends on host permissions, compatible tools and configuration. The current documentation describes a single-host application and still requires clean-host installation, upgrade and disaster-recovery acceptance checks.
status: Open-source release-candidate work. Clean-host acceptance and high-availability operation are not verified.
demonstrates: Real-time frontend/backend integration, infrastructure data modelling, access controls and recovery-aware application design.
alt: Nexora Lab dashboard showing host status, resource metrics and infrastructure health
decisions: Keeping collection behind the backend gives the interface one reporting model instead of separate rendering logic for each host integration. WebSocket updates carry changing values without repeatedly requesting an entire dashboard; persisted records serve a different purpose from live telemetry.

meta: Nexora Agent collects Linux, Docker, sensor, disk and network telemetry through isolated plugins, then reports to Nexora Lab using an outbound connection.
overview: Nexora Agent is a plugin-based Linux telemetry agent that reports host, container, sensor and disk information to Nexora Lab. It collects local details that a virtualization API cannot always provide.
problem: A virtualization API cannot expose every local temperature sensor, service state or disk-health reading. The Agent fills those gaps while allowing unsupported collectors to remain unavailable without disabling the whole application.
approach: Six collection plugins cover Linux, Docker, Proxmox, sensors, SMART disk health and networking. Plugins collect and normalize data; Agent Core handles identity, transport, retries and the versioned reporting contract. Capability detection tells the dashboard what a particular host can provide.
features: Independent collection plugins and capability detection
Host, container, sensor, disk and network data
Outbound reporting and diagnostic tools
result: The repository contains the collectors, core transport and tests for protocol, availability and reconnection behavior. Hardware-fleet deployment has not been verified.
tradeoff: Sensor and SMART coverage depend on host tools and privileges. Container visibility requires explicitly granted access; no universal hardware coverage or fixed resource-use guarantee is claimed.
status: Open-source tool under active development. Runtime support must be checked against the documented host requirements.
demonstrates: Modular Node.js/TypeScript engineering, resilient telemetry collection and clear protocol boundaries.
decisions: A plugin boundary lets a missing sensor tool affect one collector rather than the whole reporting process. Centralizing transport in Agent Core also keeps retry and identity behavior consistent across plugins. Capability reporting distinguishes unavailable data from a misleading zero reading.
problemHeading: Collecting what the host can report.

meta: CompressMe combines a PySide6 desktop interface and Python CLI for batch image compression, duplicate detection, metadata handling and exportable reports.
overview: CompressMe is a Python image compression tool for processing folders, reviewing duplicates and exporting reports. A PySide6 desktop application and command-line interface share the same batch-processing engine.
problem: Processing an image folder one file at a time makes it difficult to keep settings consistent or see which files failed. A repeatable batch workflow also needs to distinguish identical files from visually similar images.
approach: A Python compression engine supports the PySide6 interface and CLI. Exact hashing and perceptual comparison serve different duplicate-detection tasks. Reports preserve a record of processed files, size changes and failures; optional external encoders extend the available compression paths.
features: Batch processing through GUI and CLI
Exact and perceptual duplicate detection
Metadata controls and CSV, JSON or text reports
result: The public source includes the engine and desktop workflow, and the published screenshot shows queue and report presentation. Compression savings depend on the input, output settings and encoder; no universal saving percentage is claimed.
tradeoff: Image formats and external tools have different capabilities. Metadata preservation and lossy compression involve choices that should remain visible to the user.
status: Public source and releases are available. The README lists Windows and Linux support; macOS and Android are not presented as completed supported platforms.
demonstrates: Shared application logic, desktop interface development, file processing and useful operational reporting.
alt: CompressMe desktop dashboard showing a compression queue and processing reports
decisions: Sharing the compression engine between the desktop interface and CLI keeps the processing rules consistent for interactive and repeatable batch work. Exact hashes answer whether files are identical; perceptual comparison answers a different question about visual similarity. Keeping those paths separate avoids treating every similar image as a duplicate.

meta: Jenica Salazar’s client portfolio website connects professional experience, certificates, selected work and résumé access. Explore the Next.js implementation.
overview: Jenica Salazar’s client portfolio website brings her professional background, experience and MovieFlix founder story into a responsive Next.js presentation.
problem: A résumé, certificates and a separate project story can be difficult to assess when presented independently. The website gives those materials a clear sequence while keeping résumé and contact access easy to find.
approach: Next.js and React organize the page into background, experience, skills, certificates and project sections. Supplied portraits use responsive image delivery, while metadata and Person structured data support a consistent public identity.
features: Professional background, experience and certificate sections
MovieFlix founder story and résumé access
Responsive layouts and contact alternatives
result: The published website is accessible. Source review confirms the portfolio sections and a contact path that can use a server-side provider when configured, with an email-app fallback. Successful email delivery was not tested in this audit.
tradeoff: A contact interface must clearly distinguish a sent message from a prepared email. Career outcomes, employer response and conversion improvements cannot be inferred from the site being online.
status: Confirmed client work. Published professional portfolio; server-delivered contact behavior requires separate verification.
demonstrates: Content hierarchy, responsive personal branding, image delivery and accurate contact behavior.
alt: Jenica Salazar's portfolio homepage with her portrait and professional introduction
decisions: Separating experience, qualifications and project context makes different kinds of evidence easier to inspect. Responsive image delivery avoids sending the largest portrait to every screen. A contact fallback gives visitors an alternative when the server-side message provider is unavailable, but requires distinct feedback for a prepared email and a delivered message.
problemHeading: A professional story in one place.
decisionHeading: Structure the content around her work.

meta: MovieFlix organizes local media with TMDB metadata, byte-range playback and FFmpeg transcoding. Explore its self-hosted architecture and private-demo limits.
overview: MovieFlix is a self-hosted media streaming platform for organizing a local video collection and serving playback. Its library interface connects media scanning, title information and FFmpeg processing; this case study keeps the private deployment address confidential.
problem: Media files need more than a directory listing: people need recognizable titles, artwork and playback that can seek through large files. Different codecs add another compatibility challenge.
approach: The application scans local media, uses FFprobe to inspect files and TMDB to enrich titles, then serves supported playback through byte-range requests or FFmpeg processing. Next.js provides the interface and server routes, with SQLite application records and Redis-backed runtime support.
features: Library scanning and metadata enrichment
Documented HTTP 206 playback, transcoding and subtitles
Profiles and administration controls
result: Public source and documentation describe the scanning, playback and management paths. The supplied screenshot shows the library interface. Private playback, seeking and administrative operations were not exercised in this audit.
tradeoff: Playback depends on codecs, server resources and access controls. Controls can restrict requests; they do not justify a claim that copying is impossible. Media availability and rights are separate from software capability.
status: Public code with a privately hosted runtime. The public links provide source and documentation; the runtime endpoint stays private.
demonstrates: Media-processing integration, streaming route design, stateful application architecture and administration interfaces.
alt: MovieFlix library homepage showing featured artwork and media rows
decisions: Byte-range responses allow supported players to request a portion of a file when seeking instead of restarting a full download. Codec inspection informs whether direct delivery is appropriate or processing is needed. Library metadata and playback are separate concerns, so richer browsing does not depend on changing the source media files.
problemHeading: From local files to a browsable library.
decisionHeading: Separate the library from playback processing.

meta: Donut House demonstrates product discovery, custom donut boxes, saved items and checkout in a Next.js storefront. No real orders or payments are processed.
overview: Donut House is an interactive bakery storefront demonstration built with Next.js. Visitors can browse products, customize choices and follow a simulated cart and checkout journey.
problem: A custom box is more complicated than a single product purchase: choices need to remain understandable as items, quantities and options change. The design challenge is to carry those decisions from discovery into the cart without losing context.
approach: Next.js, React and TypeScript structure the storefront. Zustand manages shopping state, Zod validates structured inputs, and separate product, cart and checkout helpers keep calculations away from presentation components.
features: Catalog discovery, search, filters and saved items
Product options and a custom box builder
Persistent cart and demonstration checkout
result: The live demo is accessible, and source review confirms product/cart helpers and checkout calculations. This demonstrates a customer-facing workflow; it does not establish a bakery operation, payment integration or fulfilled order.
tradeoff: Persistent shopping state is useful, but real commerce would also require trusted server-side order handling, inventory, payment and operational policies. Those are outside this demo's verified scope.
status: Portfolio commerce concept. No real orders, payments or delivery service.
demonstrates: Connected interaction design, structured state management, validation and reusable commerce logic.
alt: Donut House storefront showing donut collections and custom box presentation
decisions: A shared cart store keeps selections consistent between the product page, box builder and checkout. Moving calculations into helpers makes quantities and totals easier to check independently of the layout. Input validation handles incomplete selections before they enter the demonstration checkout; it does not turn browser state into a trusted order record.
decisionHeading: Keep shopping state separate from presentation.

meta: Mark Jaron’s client portfolio website presents engineering experience, selected studies, certifications and résumé access in a responsive static website.
overview: Mark Jaron’s client portfolio website presents his industrial engineering experience, studies, certifications and practical toolkit in a structured professional profile.
problem: A long professional record needs clear grouping so visitors can understand responsibilities and inspect relevant work. The site turns that material into a readable professional narrative rather than copying a résumé into one uninterrupted block.
approach: Semantic HTML, CSS and JavaScript provide the layout and interactions without a framework build. The site is served statically on Vercel, with public metadata and a contact form that prepares an email in the visitor's own application.
features: Experience and selected-study presentation
Certifications, résumé and contact access
Responsive static delivery
result: The published site is accessible and the local README confirms its static deployment model. The contact form does not submit or store an inquiry through a server.
tradeoff: Static delivery keeps deployment simple; content changes are made in source rather than through a CMS. Opening an email draft is not evidence of message delivery or a client lead.
status: Confirmed client work. Published professional portfolio with an email-app contact workflow; it does not submit an inquiry to a server.
demonstrates: Editorial organization, framework-free responsive development and transparent contact UX.
alt: Mark Jaron's portfolio introduction and engineering experience presentation
decisions: Static delivery suits a presentation site whose content changes through source edits. Semantic sections establish a readable hierarchy without a framework runtime. The contact workflow uses the visitor’s email application, so the interface can prepare an inquiry without claiming a server received it.
decisionHeading: Give each part of the profile a clear place.

meta: Your Coffee presents a 33-drink menu, product customization and a locally saved cart in a static café demo. Checkout and payment are simulations.
overview: Your Coffee is a café ordering website demo with a searchable drink menu, customization options and a JavaScript shopping cart. The ordering journey demonstrates interface behavior without accepting real orders.
problem: A broad drink menu becomes harder to explore when customers also need to choose options. The interface brings discovery and customization together, while keeping the current order visible.
approach: Semantic HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript power the experience. Hash-based routing switches between product, cart and checkout views on static hosting. Only cart state is persisted locally; checkout details are not submitted to a business.
features: 33-drink catalog with search and category filters
Drink customization and browser-persisted cart
Back/forward-compatible views and demo checkout
result: The live site is accessible, and the source connects catalog, routing, customization and cart updates. Checkout and payment views demonstrate interface behavior rather than a commercial transaction.
tradeoff: Browser storage provides convenience without an account, but does not synchronize an order across devices or replace a server-side order system.
status: Portfolio café concept. No real orders or payments; personal checkout details are not transmitted.
demonstrates: Static application architecture, state persistence and customer-facing interaction design.
alt: Your Coffee café homepage showing the drink menu and ordering presentation
decisions: Hash-based routes let the static host serve one application while preserving browser back and forward navigation. Keeping the cart in browser storage retains selections between visits without an account. Limiting persistence to cart state also avoids storing checkout details as though they were submitted orders.

meta: Python-Keybr brings adaptive typing practice, WPM and accuracy feedback, saved progress and keyboard diagnostics to a Python curses terminal interface.
overview: Python-Keybr is a Python terminal typing trainer inspired by keybr.com. Its curses interface provides practice, timing feedback and keyboard diagnostics without a browser.
problem: A terminal practice tool needs to show errors and progress without interrupting typing. The project also explores adaptive practice, where weaker letters receive attention and new letters unlock as confidence improves.
approach: Python and curses handle the interface and keystroke feedback. Per-letter and bigram statistics guide adaptive practice, while local progress records support later sessions. A separate diagnostic mode inspects keyboard input behavior.
features: Six typing practice modes plus keyboard diagnostics
Live WPM, accuracy and per-letter feedback
Local progress, session statistics and adaptive letter unlocking
result: The public README and Python sources implement the practice modes, persistent statistics and diagnostic interface. No improvement in a person's typing speed is claimed without a recorded study.
tradeoff: Terminal and keyboard capabilities vary by operating system. Windows requires the documented curses dependency; advanced diagnostics have platform constraints.
status: Public terminal tool. The adaptive concept is credited to keybr.com; this is an independent implementation.
demonstrates: Terminal interface design, input handling, local persistence and adaptive application logic.
decisions: Immediate keystroke feedback belongs in the terminal loop, while accumulated statistics inform later practice. Per-letter and bigram records let adaptive sessions respond to specific weaknesses rather than only an overall score. A separate diagnostic mode makes input behavior inspectable without interrupting a practice session.
problemHeading: Useful typing feedback in a terminal.
decisionHeading: Coordinate input, timing and terminal rendering.

meta: DistroZSH provides distribution-aware themes, prompt layouts and command suggestions without a shell framework, with a documented reversible installer.
overview: DistroZSH is a lightweight Linux ZSH configuration with a distribution-aware prompt and selectable layouts. It provides a consistent shell setup without a shell framework or plugin manager.
problem: Shell customization can accumulate dependencies and changes that are difficult to undo. This project provides a defined configuration while adapting the prompt's appearance to the running distribution.
approach: ZSH prompt functions, distribution detection and shell scripts provide themes and layouts. The installer and uninstall workflow document how to apply or reverse the configuration, while command-not-found handling can suggest likely corrections.
features: Distribution-aware prompt themes and layout choices
Command suggestions and documented customization
Reversible installation without a framework dependency
result: The public repository documents the configuration and installer. Existing theme previews show the prompt engine's output; they do not establish startup speed across every supported system.
tradeoff: Distribution detection and terminal behavior can vary. Supported versions and documented fallback behavior are more useful than a universal compatibility claim.
status: Public configuration project under active development.
demonstrates: Shell scripting, environment detection and maintainable developer tooling.
decisions: Distribution detection changes presentation while the prompt functions retain a common structure. A documented uninstall path treats shell configuration as a reversible change. Avoiding a framework dependency reduces the setup required, although terminal capabilities still need to be checked.
problemHeading: A consistent prompt across Linux systems.
decisionHeading: Keep the shell setup small and configurable.

meta: An unofficial Starbucks-inspired login interface demonstrating responsive layout and client-side validation. It is a practice demo, not real authentication.
overview: Starbucks Login is an unofficial responsive login-interface demo built for frontend practice. Validation and feedback run in the browser; the page does not authenticate users against Starbucks services.
problem: A login interface needs understandable fields and clear feedback when input is incomplete or incorrect. This small project focuses on that interaction rather than account management.
approach: The portfolio publishes static HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A client-side submit handler prevents server submission and checks demonstration values, then presents success or error feedback.
features: Responsive login layout
Required fields and client-side feedback
Demonstration-only success and error states
result: The published source implements the input and feedback loop. No account is created and no identity is authenticated against a production service.
tradeoff: Client-side checks are appropriate for this demonstration but are not authentication security. A real login system would need server-side identity, session and abuse controls.
status: Unofficial, noncommissioned practice project with no Starbucks affiliation.
demonstrates: Accessible form presentation and concise frontend validation behavior.
alt: Unofficial Starbucks-inspired login form with email and password fields
decisions: Preventing the browser’s default submission keeps this exercise within its static demo boundary. Field checks and explicit error states make the interaction understandable. The success state demonstrates feedback design only; authentication belongs on a trusted server in an operational system.
problemHeading: Clear feedback in a compact form.
decisionHeading: Validate the interface without implying authentication.

meta: Smart Expense Visualizer combines expense entry, category charts, summary cards and a sortable table. Demo records stay in the browser using localStorage.
overview: Smart Expense Visualizer is a browser-based expense tracking dashboard demonstration. JavaScript records and category charts help inspect a local collection of entries without a server account.
problem: A transaction list alone makes spending patterns hard to inspect. The dashboard connects each entry to category totals, summary cards and a chart that changes with the records.
approach: JavaScript manages the records and browser storage, while Chart.js renders category totals. A sortable table complements the chart so individual transactions remain inspectable.
features: Validated expense entry and deletion
Category chart and spending summaries
Sortable transactions and local persistence
result: The published HTML and script provide the interactive record/chart workflow. Records are stored in the current browser rather than a server-side account or financial database.
tradeoff: Local storage keeps the demo simple but provides no cross-device synchronization, shared accounts or guaranteed backup. Clearing site data removes records.
status: Interactive browser demo; not a financial-accounting service. The published version loads UI libraries from CDNs.
demonstrates: Data-driven interface updates, local state persistence and visual reporting.
alt: Expense dashboard showing summary cards, a category chart and transaction table
decisions: A chart provides an overview, while the table preserves access to individual entries. Recalculating summaries from the records keeps the chart and totals aligned after deletion. Browser storage enables continuity on one device without introducing an account or implying a remote backup.
problemHeading: Seeing individual entries and category totals.
decisionHeading: Keep records inspectable alongside the chart.

meta: Monthsary is a personal anniversary website combining a time-together counter, timeline, photo galleries, video moments and letters in one intimate story.
overview: Monthsary is an interactive personal anniversary website that brings photographs, letters and shared moments into a timeline and media galleries.
problem: Personal memories deserve a coherent presentation rather than a disconnected set of files. The design challenge is to make the story easy to explore while keeping its intimate purpose intact.
approach: HTML, CSS and JavaScript connect a time-together counter with a timeline and media galleries. The visual treatment supports the story without introducing an account or commercial checkout workflow.
features: Time-together counter and personal timeline
Photo galleries, video moments and letters
Responsive presentation and light interaction
result: The published Netlify website is accessible and its content presents the personal story. No audience or commercial outcome is asserted.
tradeoff: The presentation depends on consent for the existing personal media. This case study discusses the interface without adding relationship details.
status: Published personal project. Preserve its purpose and avoid commercial framing.
demonstrates: Personal storytelling, responsive media presentation and time-based interface behavior.
alt: Monthsary anniversary website with a personal timeline and photo presentation
decisions: The counter, timeline and galleries give different entry points into the same personal story. Lightweight browser interactions support reading and exploration without needing an account. The case study stays focused on presentation rather than reproducing additional private content.
problemHeading: Make a personal story easy to explore.
decisionHeading: Let the timeline and galleries carry the story.

meta: JohnVex-WinOps organizes Windows diagnostics and allowlisted operations with dry-run planning, verification, journals and structured PowerShell output.
overview: JohnVex-WinOps is a PowerShell Windows administration toolkit that organizes diagnostics and system operations behind a modular engine. Commands follow defined checks and execution boundaries.
problem: Ad-hoc maintenance scripts can make it difficult to understand what will change, what privileges are needed and what happened afterward. The toolkit gives those operations a defined planning and logging workflow.
approach: A declarative catalog exposes allowlisted operations. Dry-run planning, explicit risk acceptance and verification surround supported changes, while JSONL logs and operation journals preserve the session record.
features: Inventory, health and network diagnostics
Allowlisted operation catalog and dry-run planning
Verification, structured logs and supported rollback journals
result: The public repository contains the engine, catalog and test/release tooling. Elevated Windows operations and organizational rollout have not been verified here.
tradeoff: Some operations require elevation and carry material risk. Rollback support is operation-specific, not a promise that every action can be undone. Third-party functionality remains subject to its documented boundaries.
status: Public administration toolkit with edition boundaries described in its documentation.
demonstrates: PowerShell automation, explicit operational controls and auditable application behavior.
alt: JohnVex-WinOps administration interface showing diagnostic and operation options
decisions: An allowlisted catalog makes the available operations explicit before execution. Planning and risk acceptance precede changes, while verification and logs describe what happened afterward. Operation-specific journals provide a recovery path where implemented instead of promising universal rollback.

meta: J&GLO demonstrates collection filters, product variants, image galleries and a locally saved shopping bag in a fictional Next.js fashion storefront.
overview: J&GLO is a fictional Next.js fashion storefront with product variants, collection pages and an interactive shopping bag. Its editorial presentation supports browsing and simulated shopping rather than live commerce.
problem: Campaign imagery and a usable catalog have different jobs. The design challenge is to preserve the fashion identity while making variants, sizes and the current shopping bag understandable.
approach: Next.js and React organize collection and product routes. Catalog and cart helpers define variants and totals, while a shared store provider validates browser-persisted cart and wishlist state. Custom CSS and Motion support the presentation.
features: Collection search, filters and sorting
Product galleries, color and size selection
Editable shopping bag and local wishlist persistence
result: The live storefront is accessible and source review confirms the catalog, cart helpers and storage boundary. Products, imagery and commerce policies are illustrative; no real order or payment is created.
tradeoff: The demo does not provide a commerce backend, real stock or customer accounts. Locally persisted item selections demonstrate continuity, not production order management.
status: Published fictional storefront demo. Contact and newsletter responses are local previews, not delivered submissions.
demonstrates: Product interaction design, reusable state logic and editorial frontend presentation.
alt: J&GLO fictional fashion storefront with campaign imagery and garment collections
decisions: Product routes preserve room for the campaign presentation while cart helpers handle variants, quantities and totals. Validating persisted state prevents stale browser data from being accepted blindly when the catalog changes. The shared provider connects those behaviors without making individual presentation components responsible for storage.
problemHeading: Connect editorial presentation with shopping state.
decisionHeading: Define variants and totals in shared helpers.

meta: ARKOSENYO is a client architecture website project with service pages, project search, filters and galleries. Explore the implemented website demonstration.
overview: ARKOSENYO is a client architecture website development project presenting services, project records and image galleries. The published demonstration includes search and filtering for exploring the work.
problem: An architecture website needs to connect project discovery with services and a clear inquiry path. I organized the client’s project material so visitors can filter work, open its details and explore imagery without losing context.
approach: The reviewed source uses Next.js, React and TypeScript with structured project records. Service and project routes share a display model; search, filters, keyboard-accessible galleries and an inquiry draft support exploration.
features: Project search, filters and detail galleries
Connected services and project routes
Responsive imagery and inquiry-draft interactions
result: The published demonstration is accessible. Reviewed source includes service and project routes, project filtering, galleries and an inquiry-draft interaction. A live inquiry delivery integration has not been verified.
tradeoff: Source-managed project records keep lists and detail pages consistent. Editorial accounts, approvals and a business CMS would require additional implementation; they are not claimed as delivered.
status: Client website project. The available link is a website demonstration; a separate production launch is not asserted.
demonstrates: Content modelling, editorial website design, accessible galleries and responsive delivery.
alt: ARKOSENYO redesign concept presenting architecture imagery and project discovery
decisions: Structured records let project lists, filters and detail routes use the same content model. Keeping an inquiry as a draft avoids suggesting a server accepted it. The model is suitable for a source-managed concept; adding editorial permissions and publishing workflows would be a separate CMS implementation.
problemHeading: Make architecture projects easier to explore.
decisionHeading: Use structured records for search and galleries.

meta: TAITECH Marine is a client website redesign with equipment browsing, service details, galleries and a conditional request preview. View the implementation.
overview: TAITECH Marine is a client marine-equipment business website redesign project. Its published demonstration combines equipment and service presentation with search, galleries and a structured request preview.
problem: Equipment and service inquiries need useful context. I connected category browsing with a request flow that asks relevant questions and lets visitors review their details before the demonstration confirmation.
approach: Next.js, React and TypeScript provide static content routes, category views and native-dialog galleries. A six-step request preview changes its questions with the selected request type, then offers editable review and a demonstration confirmation.
features: Equipment/project search and category filtering
Service details and accessible image galleries
Conditional request steps with review and local preview
result: The published demonstration is accessible. Reviewed source includes content routes, category filtering, gallery controls and the request validator. Confirmation is a frontend preview; delivery, scheduling and reserved availability have not been verified.
tradeoff: The request flow demonstrates conditional fields and review states. Operational submission, scheduling, notifications and administration would need their own implemented integrations and acceptance checks.
status: Client website project. The request preview does not send an inquiry, book a meeting or reserve availability.
demonstrates: Structured business content, conditional form design and responsive industrial presentation.
alt: TAITECH Marine redesign demonstration showing equipment and technical service presentation
decisions: Conditional questions keep irrelevant fields out of a request path. A review step lets a visitor inspect and edit the assembled information before seeing the preview confirmation. This demonstrates form design without pretending that availability, scheduling or message delivery exists behind it.
decisionHeading: Connect browsing with a structured request preview.

meta: Shoes on the Go combines scroll-directed scenes, model rotation, camera presets and material variants using Three.js, React Three Fiber and GSAP.
overview: Shoes on the Go is an interactive 3D product showcase built with Three.js and React Three Fiber. A directed footwear story leads into rotation, variants and inspection controls.
problem: A product presentation needs to show form and detail while still letting visitors explore it themselves. The project tests how cinematic scrolling and direct manipulation can share one model.
approach: One persistent React Three Fiber canvas holds the model. GSAP directs narrative progress, while a separate interaction group handles rotation, variants and inspection. Camera presets and explicit touch controls make exploration available beyond pointer dragging.
features: Reversible scroll-directed scenes
Rotation, zoom, camera presets and material variants
Wireframe inspection and responsive control alternatives
result: The live experience is accessible and the source documents the rendering and control architecture. The shoe is a licensed sample asset, not a product designed or sold by the portfolio owner.
tradeoff: The supplied model is a unified mesh, so the experience does not fabricate an exploded assembly. GPU capability and reduced-motion behavior are part of delivering the interaction responsibly.
status: Personal, noncommercial concept with no manufacturer affiliation, store or checkout. Preserve the original asset attribution.
demonstrates: Real-time 3D frontend engineering, camera choreography and interaction ownership.
alt: Shoes on the Go 3D footwear presentation with model inspection controls
decisions: A persistent canvas avoids rebuilding the scene between narrative chapters. Separating scroll direction from direct manipulation lets visitors inspect the same object without losing the presentation structure. Camera presets and touch controls provide alternatives when dragging is inconvenient.
problemHeading: Move from a product story to inspection.
decisionHeading: Keep narrative and exploration controls distinct.

meta: ARCHÉON presents an original house concept through nine construction stages, floor plans, camera controls and material choices. Briefs download locally.
overview: ARCHÉON is an interactive 3D architecture visualization of an original tropical-modern house concept. Visitors can move through reversible construction stages and explore concept floor plans.
problem: A finished rendering hides the relationship between structure, spaces and finishes. The concept helps visitors explore those relationships through staged assembly, viewpoints and room information.
approach: Next.js, React Three Fiber, Three.js and GSAP connect nine construction stages with camera controls. A component model records stage, floor, dimensions and materials; repeated shapes can be rendered together to reduce draw work. The 3D section loads near the point where it is needed.
features: Nine reversible construction stages and chapter controls
Floor selection, concept plans, lighting and material choices
Camera presets, exploration mode and local project-brief download
result: The live demo is accessible and local source confirms the component model, floor-plan interface and text-draft download. The form validates and prepares a brief; it does not send an enquiry, issue a quotation or book a meeting.
tradeoff: The house and plans are illustrative, not an engineered design or construction specification. Rendering prioritizes interactive explanation; WebGL fallback and reduced-motion paths are documented separately.
status: Original frontend demonstration. Amihan House is not a completed commission; no server-side brief storage or submission occurs.
demonstrates: Original component-based 3D modelling, scroll choreography, progressive loading and clear form boundaries.
alt: ARCHÉON Amihan House concept showing a construction stage and exploration controls
decisions: Stage and floor information in the component model connects construction chapters with the plan interface. Rendering repeated shapes together reduces repeated draw work, while loading the 3D section near its use avoids making it the first requirement for reading the page. Local brief download keeps the form useful within an explicitly frontend-only boundary.
problemHeading: Explain a house through its construction stages.
decisionHeading: Connect reversible chapters with floor exploration.
